summary: Exploratory two-library case study: GPT-4o generates Alloy specs separately from a README and from source code, then pytest tests from each spec, with no manual correction and three runs per prompt. On Flipper (feature flags) the README-derived spec models name uniqueness as a checkable predicate and yields a test exposing that create() accepts duplicate names, which a direct README-to-pytest baseline (37 passing tests, 68% branch coverage) never catches; on Cerberus the code-derived spec captures a sized-type abstraction giving two extra tests.

claims.claim: GPT-4o produced syntactically valid Alloy and executable tests in every run without manual correction
claims.evidence: §III-C/D and §IV; 2 libraries x 2 sources x 3 runs = 12 spec generations; Alloy Analyzer checks not detailed beyond validity statement.

claims.claim: The Alloy pipeline found a genuine Flipper bug (duplicate names accepted) the existing suite and direct baseline missed
claims.evidence: §IV-B-IV-D, Table I: README spec 1 failing test in all 3 runs; baseline 0/3. 'Genuine bug' is the authors' reading of one README sentence; not yet reported to or confirmed by maintainers (§V-C). Single defect.

claims.claim: A formal intermediate representation surfaces constraint-level defects that coverage-oriented generation misses
claims.evidence: Generalization from one bug in one library; baseline prompt was not instructed to test documented invariants, so the comparison partly measures prompt focus.

claims.claim: Code-derived specs give lower test-count variance (mean SD 2.15 vs 5.0)
claims.evidence: Table II over 3 runs x 2 libraries; test count is acknowledged as a weak metric; authors flag generalization as open.

claims.claim: Doc- and code-derived specs are complementary (pred vs fact divergence signals drift)
claims.evidence: Flipper pred/fact divergence (§IV-B) and Cerberus SizedVal abstraction producing two extra tests (§IV-E); anecdotal.

patterns.note: LLM-generated Alloy specs as an intermediate for test derivation; proof-of-concept on two libraries.
Spec-first test derivation from requirements documentation; spec-vs-code divergence as drift signal.
Making a documented requirement an explicit checkable predicate is what exposed the defect; weak (single case).
Tests derived from spec rather than implementation; not a TDD loop.

methodology.sample: 2 Python libraries (Flipper, Cerberus), selected for constraints that translate naturally into Alloy; 3 runs per prompt
methodology.baselines: one direct README-to-pytest prompt (Flipper only); existing test suites
methodology.variance: 3 runs; SD of test counts reported (Table II)
methodology.ablations: README-spec vs code-spec 'micro ablation' on Flipper (Table I)
methodology.contamination_controls: none; both libraries and READMEs are public and possibly in training data

standards.artifacts: prompts printed in paper; no pipeline code or generated specs/tests repository found

biases.detail: Two libraries, one bug, three runs.
Subjects chosen for 'clear and localised validation logic' that maps naturally to Alloy.
Direct baseline not asked to test documented invariants; no comparison to property-based testing or a structured-requirements prompt without Alloy.
Duplicate-name 'bug' not confirmed by maintainers; could be intended overwrite semantics.

verdict_reason: Interesting idea honestly framed as proof-of-concept, but evidence is one unconfirmed bug in one library, one model, Python only, and a weak baseline; the deterministic gate will reject at rigor 1, which is appropriate.
applicability: Conceptually relevant to spec-driven development: deriving tests from the written requirement (not the implementation) and comparing a doc-derived spec with a code-derived one to detect drift. For a Java ingestion/delivery team, the lighter-weight transfer is to have agents turn each documented invariant (unique content IDs, required metadata fields, valid enum values across the >=4 ingestion repos) into an explicit checkable predicate and a JUnit test, without necessarily adopting Alloy. Evidence is far too thin to justify adding a formal-methods step to the harness.
